expectedText:
DISPOSITION OF PERSONAL PROPERTY REMAINING ON THE PREMISES AFTER TENANCY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan Lee

PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet states California law on what happens to personal property that Jordan Lee ("the former tenant") leaves behind at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 after a tenancy there has terminated and the premises have been vacated, under California Civil Code Chapter 5 of Title 5 of the Civil Code, Civil Code §§ 1980–1991. That chapter creates an optional statutory procedure landlords may use for handling personal property a former tenant does not take when leaving; a landlord's use of this procedure is not the only way California law allows a landlord to handle such property, and this document does not determine that Acme Properties, LLC has used, will use, or must use this procedure for the property left at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 after Jordan Lee's tenancy there ended on or about August 31, 2026. This chapter does not apply to manufactured homes, mobilehomes, or commercial coaches as those terms are defined in the Health and Safety Code, to property a landlord reasonably believes to be lost rather than left behind at the end of a tenancy, to certain animals, or to certain other categories of property addressed by other statutes, each described further in this document. This document states California statutory law as of the date signed below. It does not determine that any specific item of property found at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 is covered by this chapter, does not determine the value of any specific item, and does not determine that any specific notice, storage, or disposal step described in this document has been or will be carried out correctly in a specific case.

DEFINITIONS UNDER THIS CHAPTER
Civil Code § 1980 defines several terms "as used in this chapter" — meaning these definitions govern only Civil Code §§ 1980–1991 and are not necessarily the meanings the same words carry elsewhere in California law. "Landlord" means any operator, keeper, lessor, or sublessor of any furnished or unfurnished premises for hire, or that person's agent or successor in interest. "Owner" means any person other than the landlord who has any right, title, or interest in the personal property. "Premises" includes any common areas associated with the rented space. "Tenant" includes any paying guest, lessee, or sublessee of any premises for hire. "Reasonable belief" means the actual knowledge or belief a prudent person would have without making an investigation, including any investigation of public records, except that where the landlord has specific information indicating that such an investigation would more probably than not reveal pertinent information and the cost would be reasonable relative to the property's probable value, "reasonable belief" includes what a prudent person would have known or believed had that investigation been made.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Landlord” means any operator, keeper, lessor, or sublessor of any furnished or unfurnished premises for hire, or his or her agent or successor in interest."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1980(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, definition of "Landlord" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1980.)
  "“Owner” means any person other than the landlord who has any right, title, or interest in personal property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1980(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, definition of "Owner" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1980.)
  "“Premises” includes any common areas associated therewith."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1980(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, definition of "Premises" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1980.)
  "“Tenant” includes any paying guest, lessee, or sublessee of any premises for hire."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1980(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, definition of "Tenant" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1980.)
  "“Reasonable belief” means the actual knowledge or belief a prudent person would have without making an investigation (including any investigation of public records)"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1980(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, definition of "Reasonable belief" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1980.)
  Known gap: Civil Code § 1980 defines "Premises" only by stating that it "includes any common areas associated therewith" — the statute does not itself supply a general definition of the primary term. These definitions apply only within this chapter; other California statutes governing landlord-tenant relationships (for example, the unlawful detainer statutes) define "tenant" and related terms separately, and this document does not state whether or how those definitions differ.

AN OPTIONAL PROCEDURE, AND WHAT THIS CHAPTER DOES NOT COVER
Civil Code § 1981 states that this chapter "provides an optional procedure for the disposition of personal property that remains on the premises after a tenancy has terminated and the premises have been vacated by the tenant." The chapter does not apply whenever certain other statutes apply instead (Civil Code §§ 1862.5, 2080.8, 2080.9, or 2081 to 2081.6), and it does not apply to property that exists for the purpose of providing utility services and is owned by a public utility. It also does not apply to any manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial coach as those terms are defined in the Health and Safety Code, including attachments to or contents of those structures, regardless of whether the structure is subject to registration — nor does it apply to the disposition of certain animals covered by other statutes. Separately, Civil Code § 1982 directs that personal property a landlord reasonably believes to have been lost (as opposed to left behind at the end of a tenancy) must instead be handled under the general lost-property statutes beginning at Civil Code § 2080; a landlord who complies with that separate statute is not liable to the property's owner on account of that property. If the local police or sheriff's department refuses to accept property offered to it as lost property under that statute, the landlord may instead dispose of the property under this chapter.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This chapter provides an optional procedure for the disposition of personal property that remains on the premises after a tenancy has terminated and the premises have been vacated by the tenant."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1981(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, this chapter as an optional procedure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1981.)
  "This chapter does not apply to any manufactured home as defined in Section 18007 of the Health and Safety Code, any mobilehome as defined in Section 18008 of the Health and Safety Code, or to any commercial coach as defined in Section 18001.8 of the Health and Safety Code, including attachments thereto or contents thereof, whether or not the manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial coach is subject to registration under the Health and Safety Code."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1981(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, exclusion of manufactured homes, mobilehomes, and commercial coaches (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1981.)
  "If the requirements of this chapter are not satisfied, nothing in this chapter affects the rights and liabilities of the landlord, former tenant, or any other person."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1981(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, effect of noncompliance with this chapter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1981.)
  "Personal property which the landlord reasonably believes to have been lost shall be disposed of pursuant to Article 1 (commencing with Section 2080) of Chapter 4 of Title 6. The landlord is not liable to the owner of the property if he complies with this subdivision. (b) If the appropriate police or sheriff’s department refuses to accept property pursuant to subdivision (a), the landlord may dispose of the property pursuant to this chapter."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1982(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, property reasonably believed to be lost (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1982.)
  Known gap: Civil Code § 1981(e) states that if this chapter's requirements are not satisfied, "nothing in this chapter affects the rights and liabilities of the landlord, former tenant, or any other person" — meaning this chapter is a safe-harbor procedure a landlord may choose to follow, not the exclusive framework governing what happens to property left behind. Because manufactured homes, mobilehomes, and commercial coaches are expressly excluded from this chapter, a tenancy involving one of those structures is governed by different statutes not addressed in this document. This document also does not determine, for any specific item of property, whether a landlord's belief that the item was lost (triggering § 1982) rather than left behind at the end of a tenancy (triggering the rest of this chapter) is factually correct.

NOTICE TO THE FORMER TENANT AND OTHER OWNERS: CONTENTS, TIMING, AND DELIVERY
Under Civil Code § 1983(a), where personal property remains on the premises after a tenancy has terminated and the premises have been vacated, the landlord must give written notice to the former tenant and to any other person the landlord reasonably believes to be the owner of the property; if the property consists of records, the former tenant is presumed to be their owner for purposes of this chapter. Under § 1983(b), the notice must describe the property in a manner reasonably adequate to permit its owner to identify it — though a locked, fastened, or tied container that deters immediate access to its contents may be described as such without describing what is inside — and must advise the recipient that reasonable storage costs may be charged before the property is returned, where it may be claimed, and the date by which it must be claimed. That date must be no less than 15 days after the notice is personally delivered, or, if mailed, no less than 18 days after the notice is deposited in the mail. Under § 1983(c), the notice must be personally delivered or sent by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to the recipient's last known address, and also to any other address known to the landlord where the recipient may reasonably be expected to receive it if there is reason to believe the first address will not reach them; a copy mailed to the former tenant must also be sent to the vacated premises; and if the former tenant provided the landlord with an email address, the landlord may also send the notice by email.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Where personal property remains on the premises after a tenancy has terminated and the premises have been vacated by the tenant, the landlord shall give written notice to the tenant and to any other person the landlord reasonably believes to be the owner of the property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1983(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, duty to give written notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1983.)
  "The date specified in the notice shall be a date not less than 15 days after the notice is personally delivered or, if mailed, not less than 18 days after the notice is deposited in the mail."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1983(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, required notice contents and the 15/18-day deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1983.)
  "If the former tenant provided the landlord with the tenant’s email address, the landlord may also send the notice by email."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1983(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, permitted methods of delivery, including optional email (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1983.)
  Known gap: Civil Code § 1983(b) ties the adequacy of the property description directly to the liability limitation available under § 1989 — that limitation does not protect a landlord for property not described in the notice, except for the locked-container exception — so whether a given description is "reasonably adequate" can affect a landlord's later liability, and this document does not evaluate the adequacy of any specific description. The statute allows email notice only as an addition ("may also send") where the former tenant provided an email address; it does not make email a substitute for personal delivery or mail, and does not address notice to an other-than-tenant owner by email at all.

THE STATUTORY NOTICE FORMS AND THE REQUIRED DISCLOSURE STATEMENT
Civil Code § 1984(a) sets out a form of notice titled "Notice of Right to Reclaim Abandoned Property" that, if given to the former tenant in substantially that form, satisfies § 1983's requirements. Under § 1984(b), that notice must also contain one of two statements, depending on how the landlord intends to proceed: a public-sale statement disclosing that unclaimed property will be sold at public sale after published notice, that the recipient has the right to bid at that sale, and that after the sale and deduction of storage, advertising, and sale costs, the remaining money is paid to the county and may be claimed within one year; or, alternatively, a statement that because the property is believed to be worth less than $700, it may be kept, sold, or destroyed without further notice if not reclaimed in time. Civil Code § 1985 sets out a separate statutory notice form for use when the person being notified is not the former tenant but someone else the landlord reasonably believes to be an owner of the property; a notice given in substantially that form likewise satisfies § 1983.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A notice given to the former tenant which is in substantially the following form satisfies the requirements of Section 1983: Notice of Right to Reclaim Abandoned Property"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1984(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the statutory notice form's title and function (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1984.)
  "“If you fail to reclaim the property, it will be sold at a public sale after notice of the sale has been given by publication. You have the right to bid on the property at this sale. After the property is sold and the cost of storage, advertising, and sale is deducted, the remaining money will be paid over to the county. You may claim the remaining money at any time within one year after the county receives the money.”"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1984(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the required public-sale disclosure statement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1984.)
  "“Because this property is believed to be worth less than $700, it may be kept, sold, or destroyed without further notice if you fail to reclaim it within the time indicated above.”"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1984(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the required under-$700 disclosure statement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1984.)
  "A notice which is in substantially the following form given to a person (other than the former tenant) the landlord reasonably believes to be the owner of personal property satisfies the requirements of Section 1983"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1985 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the statutory form for a non-tenant owner (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1985.)
  Known gap: Both statutory forms need only be followed "in substantially" the form set out in the statute, not verbatim — California law does not define how much deviation from the printed form remains "substantial" compliance, and this document does not resolve that question for any specific notice. The two disclosure statements in § 1984(b) are mutually exclusive alternatives tied to which disposal path under § 1988 applies to the property; this document does not determine which statement applies to any specific item of property, since that turns on the landlord's reasonable belief about the property's resale value, a factual determination this document does not make.

STORING THE PROPERTY PENDING RELEASE OR DISPOSAL
Civil Code § 1986 requires that personal property described in the notice either be left on the vacated premises or be stored by the landlord in a place of safekeeping until the landlord either releases it under Civil Code § 1987 or disposes of it under Civil Code § 1988. The landlord must exercise reasonable care in storing the property, but is not liable to the tenant or any other owner for any loss that was not caused by the landlord's own deliberate or negligent act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The personal property described in the notice shall either be left on the vacated premises or be stored by the landlord in a place of safekeeping until the landlord either releases the property pursuant to Section 1987 or disposes of the property pursuant to Section 1988."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1986 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the storage duty and standard of care (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1986.)
  "The landlord shall exercise reasonable care in storing the property, but he is not liable to the tenant or any other owner for any loss not caused by his deliberate or negligent act."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1986 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the limit on the landlord's liability for stored property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1986.)
  Known gap: Civil Code § 1986 has not been amended since its original 1974 enactment, even though several neighboring sections of this same chapter were amended as recently as 2012 — it does not define "place of safekeeping," does not set a minimum storage standard beyond "reasonable care," and does not address modern storage arrangements such as third-party self-storage facilities. Whether a particular storage location or method meets the "reasonable care" standard in a specific case is a factual question this document does not resolve.

RELEASING THE PROPERTY: STORAGE COST, THE TWO-DAY WINDOW, AND HOW COST IS ASSESSED
Civil Code § 1987(a) requires the landlord to release the described property to the former tenant or, at the landlord's option, to another person reasonably believed to be its owner, if that person pays the reasonable cost of storage and takes possession by the date specified in the notice. Under § 1987(b), if the property was not released and the notice stated it would be sold at public sale, the landlord must still release it to the former tenant if the tenant claims it before the sale and pays the reasonable costs of storage, advertising, and sale incurred up to that point. Under § 1987(c), notwithstanding subdivision (a), the landlord must release the property to the former tenant without charging for storage if the property remained in the dwelling and the former tenant or reasonably-believed owner reclaims it within two days of vacating. Civil Code § 1990 governs how storage costs are assessed: a former tenant reclaiming property may be required to pay the reasonable costs of storage for all property remaining at the end of the tenancy that are unpaid at the time of the claim, while an owner other than the former tenant may be required to pay only for storage of the property in which that owner claims an interest; the landlord may not charge more than one person for the same costs; and if the landlord stores the property on the premises, the cost of storage is the fair rental value of the space reasonably required for that storage, with no cost assessed at all if the former tenant reclaims property stored on the premises within two days of vacating.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The personal property described in the notice shall be released by the landlord to the former tenant or, at the landlord’s option, to any person reasonably believed by the landlord to be its owner if that tenant or other person pays the reasonable cost of storage and takes possession of the property not later than the date specified in the notice for taking possession."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1987(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, release of property upon payment of storage cost (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1987.)
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (a), the landlord shall release the personal property described in the notice to the former tenant and shall not require the former tenant to pay the cost of storage if the property remained in the dwelling and the former tenant or other person reasonably believed by the landlord to be its owner reclaims the property within two days of vacating the dwelling."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1987(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the two-day free-reclaim window (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1987.)
  "Where a former tenant claims property pursuant to Section 1987, he or she may be required to pay the reasonable costs of storage for all the personal property remaining on the premises at the termination of the tenancy which are unpaid at the time the claim is made. (2) Where an owner other than the former tenant claims property pursuant to Section 1987, he or she may be required to pay the reasonable costs of storage for only the property in which he or she claims an interest."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1990(a)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, how storage costs are assessed between a former tenant and another owner (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1990.)
  "If the landlord stores the personal property on the premises, the cost of storage shall be the fair rental value of the space reasonably required for that storage for the term of the storage."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1990(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, storage cost when the property is stored on the premises (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1990.)
  Known gap: Neither § 1987 nor § 1990 sets a dollar figure or formula for "reasonable cost of storage" beyond tying on-premises storage to "the fair rental value of the space reasonably required" — this document does not calculate or estimate a specific dollar amount for any specific situation. The two-day free-reclaim rule in § 1987(c) applies where the property "remained in the dwelling"; the statute does not address whether that rule still applies if the landlord moved the property to off-site storage before the two days elapsed, and this document does not resolve that unaddressed situation.

DISPOSAL ONCE THE NOTICE PERIOD EXPIRES: PUBLIC SALE OR LOW-VALUE RETENTION
Civil Code § 1988(a) provides that personal property not released under § 1987 must be sold at public sale by competitive bidding — unless the landlord reasonably believes the total resale value of the unreleased property is less than $700, in which case the landlord may instead retain the property for personal use or dispose of it in any manner. The statute expressly permits the landlord or the tenant to bid on the property at the public sale. Under § 1988(b), notice of the time and place of a public sale must be published under Government Code § 6066 in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the sale will be held, with the last publication no less than five days before the sale, and that sale notice cannot be published before the deadline date specified in the § 1983 notice; the sale notice must describe the property adequately for its owner to identify it, subject to the same locked-container exception as the § 1983 notice. Under § 1988(c), after deducting the costs of storage, advertising, and sale, any unclaimed balance of the sale proceeds must be paid into the treasury of the county where the sale took place no later than 30 days after the sale; the former tenant or other owner may claim that balance within one year of the county's receipt of it by applying to the county treasurer or other designated county official, and if the county pays the balance to a claimant, neither the county nor its officers or employees are liable to any other claimant for the amount paid.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "If the personal property described in the notice is not released pursuant to Section 1987, it shall be sold at public sale by competitive bidding. However, if the landlord reasonably believes that the total resale value of the property not released is less than seven hundred dollars ($700), the landlord may retain the property for his or her own use or dispose of it in any manner."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1988(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, public sale requirement and the under-$700 exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1988.)
  "Notice of the time and place of the public sale shall be given by publication pursuant to Section 6066 of the Government Code in a newspaper of general circulation published in the county where the sale is to be held. The last publication shall be not less than five days before the sale is to be held."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1988(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, publication requirements for the sale notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1988.)
  "After deduction of the costs of storage, advertising, and sale, any balance of the proceeds of the sale which is not claimed by the former tenant or an owner other than such tenant shall be paid into the treasury of the county in which the sale took place not later than 30 days after the date of sale. The former tenant or other owner may claim the balance within one year from the date of payment to the county by making application to the county treasurer or other official designated by the county."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1988(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, disposition of unclaimed sale proceeds and the one-year claim period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1988.)
  Known gap: The $700 resale-value threshold in § 1988(a) is a fixed dollar figure as last amended effective January 1, 2013 — the statute does not index it for inflation or provide for automatic adjustment, so the same $700 figure has applied without change since that date. Whether the landlord's belief that a specific item's total resale value is under $700 is itself "reasonable" is a factual determination this document does not make.

LANDLORD'S LIMITATION OF LIABILITY, AND COORDINATION WITH A NOTICE OF BELIEF OF ABANDONMENT
Civil Code § 1989 limits a landlord's liability for property handled under this chapter. Under § 1989(a), a landlord who releases property to the former tenant is not liable with respect to that property to any person. Under § 1989(b), a landlord who releases property under § 1987 to a reasonably-believed owner other than the former tenant is not liable to anyone who was given notice under § 1983, nor to anyone who was not given notice unless that person proves the landlord believed or reasonably should have believed they had an interest in the property and also knew or reasonably should have known their address. Section 1989(c) applies the identical two-part rule to property disposed of under § 1988. Separately, Civil Code § 1991 addresses how the notice required by this chapter interacts with a notice of belief of abandonment given under the different statute at Civil Code § 1951.3: where a landlord gives a tenant a notice of belief of abandonment under § 1951.3, the notice required by § 1983 of this chapter may — but need not — be given at the same time, even though the tenancy does not terminate until the period specified in the abandonment notice ends; and if both notices are given, they may, but need not, be combined into a single notice containing all the information each underlying statute requires.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 1981, where the landlord releases to the former tenant property which remains on the premises after a tenancy is terminated, the landlord is not liable with respect to that property to any person."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1989(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, no liability after release to the former tenant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1989.)
  "Where the landlord releases property pursuant to Section 1987 to a person (other than the former tenant) reasonably believed by the landlord to be the owner of the property, the landlord is not liable with respect to that property to:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1989(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, no liability after release to a reasonably-believed owner (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1989.)
  "Any person to whom notice was not given pursuant to Section 1983 unless such person proves that, prior to disposing of the property pursuant to Section 1988, the landlord believed or reasonably should have believed that such person had an interest in the property and also that the landlord knew or should have known upon reasonable investigation the address of such person."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1989(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the two-part proof required of an unnoticed claimant after disposal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1989.)
  "Where a notice of belief of abandonment is given to a lessee pursuant to Section 1951.3, the notice to the former tenant given pursuant to Section 1983 may, but need not, be given at the same time as the notice of belief of abandonment even though the tenancy is not terminated until the end of the period specified in the notice of belief of abandonment."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1991 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, coordinating this chapter's notice with a § 1951.3 notice of belief of abandonment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1991.)
  Known gap: Every liability limitation in § 1989 protects only a landlord who has actually satisfied this chapter's requirements; under § 1981(e), noncompliance leaves the landlord's underlying rights and liabilities unaffected by this chapter, so this document does not determine whether any specific notice, storage, or disposal step was carried out correctly in a way that would trigger § 1989's protection. Civil Code § 1951.3's own notice-of-belief-of-abandonment requirements are governed by a separate statute this document does not itself state in full; § 1991's permission to combine notices is optional and does not excuse compliance with either statute's individual requirements.

NOTICE OF RIGHT TO RECLAIM ABANDONED PROPERTY — WORKSHEET AND SIGNATURE
NOTICE OF RIGHT TO RECLAIM ABANDONED PROPERTY (prepared with reference to the statutory form at Civil Code § 1984)

To: Jordan Lee, formerly of 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814.

When you vacated the premises at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 on or about August 31, 2026, the following personal property remained: One dresser, two boxes of books, a floor lamp.

You may claim this property at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814. If you fail to claim this property by September 20, 2026, unless you pay the landlord's reasonable cost of storage for the above-described property and take possession of the property you claim not later than that date, this property may be disposed of under Civil Code § 1988.

Landlord's own recordkeeping notes on the statement required by Civil Code § 1984(b) (select the one that applies and complete accordingly — the two statements are alternatives, not both): (1) public-sale statement, if the property will be sold at public sale after published notice; or (2) under-$700 statement, if the property's reasonably-believed total resale value is $150 and is therefore stated to be less than $700. Only one of these two statements is included in the notice actually given, as Civil Code § 1984(b) requires.

Dated: September 2, 2026
Signature of Acme Properties, LLC: _______________________
Type or print name: Acme Properties, LLC
Address: 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814

This worksheet is a recordkeeping aid for use in preparing a notice under Civil Code §§ 1983–1985. It does not determine that the property described is actually covered by Civil Code §§ 1980–1991, does not determine which of the two required disclosure statements applies, and does not itself constitute the notice required by statute unless completed and delivered in the manner Civil Code § 1983 describes.

Executed on September 2, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

That chapter creates an optional statutory procedure landlords may use for handling personal property a former tenant does not take when leaving; a landlord's use of this procedure is not the only way California law allows a landlord to handle such property, and this document does not determine that Acme Properties, LLC has used, will use, or must use this procedure for the property left at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 after Jordan Lee's tenancy there ended on or about August 31, 2026. Civil Code § 1980 defines several terms "as used in this chapter" — meaning these definitions govern only Civil Code §§ 1980–1991 and are not necessarily the meanings the same words carry elsewhere in California law. "Landlord" means any operator, keeper, lessor, or sublessor of any furnished or unfurnished premises for hire, or that person's agent or successor in interest. "Owner" means any person other than the landlord who has any right, title, or interest in the personal property. "Premises" includes any common areas associated with the rented space. "Tenant" includes any paying guest, lessee, or sublessee of any premises for hire. "Reasonable belief" means the actual knowledge or belief a prudent person would have without making an investigation, including any investigation of public records, except that where the landlord has specific information indicating that such an investigation would more probably than not reveal pertinent information and the cost would be reasonable relative to the property's probable value, "reasonable belief" includes what a prudent person would have known or believed had that investigation been made.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 1981 states that this chapter "provides an optional procedure for the disposition of personal property that remains on the premises after a tenancy has terminated and the premises have been vacated by the tenant." The chapter does not apply whenever certain other statutes apply instead (Civil Code §§ 1862.5, 2080.8, 2080.9, or 2081 to 2081.6), and it does not apply to property that exists for the purpose of providing utility services and is owned by a public utility. It also does not apply to any manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial coach as those terms are defined in the Health and Safety Code, including attachments to or contents of those structures, regardless of whether the structure is subject to registration — nor does it apply to the disposition of certain animals covered by other statutes. Separately, Civil Code § 1982 directs that personal property a landlord reasonably believes to have been lost (as opposed to left behind at the end of a tenancy) must instead be handled under the general lost-property statutes beginning at Civil Code § 2080; a landlord who complies with that separate statute is not liable to the property's owner on account of that property. If the local police or sheriff's department refuses to accept property offered to it as lost property under that statute, the landlord may instead dispose of the property under this chapter.

expectedJSON.body: Under Civil Code § 1983(a), where personal property remains on the premises after a tenancy has terminated and the premises have been vacated, the landlord must give written notice to the former tenant and to any other person the landlord reasonably believes to be the owner of the property; if the property consists of records, the former tenant is presumed to be their owner for purposes of this chapter. Under § 1983(b), the notice must describe the property in a manner reasonably adequate to permit its owner to identify it — though a locked, fastened, or tied container that deters immediate access to its contents may be described as such without describing what is inside — and must advise the recipient that reasonable storage costs may be charged before the property is returned, where it may be claimed, and the date by which it must be claimed. That date must be no less than 15 days after the notice is personally delivered, or, if mailed, no less than 18 days after the notice is deposited in the mail. Under § 1983(c), the notice must be personally delivered or sent by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to the recipient's last known address, and also to any other address known to the landlord where the recipient may reasonably be expected to receive it if there is reason to believe the first address will not reach them; a copy mailed to the former tenant must also be sent to the vacated premises; and if the former tenant provided the landlord with an email address, the landlord may also send the notice by email.

The statute allows email notice only as an addition ("may also send") where the former tenant provided an email address; it does not make email a substitute for personal delivery or mail, and does not address notice to an other-than-tenant owner by email at all.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 1984(a) sets out a form of notice titled "Notice of Right to Reclaim Abandoned Property" that, if given to the former tenant in substantially that form, satisfies § 1983's requirements. Under § 1984(b), that notice must also contain one of two statements, depending on how the landlord intends to proceed: a public-sale statement disclosing that unclaimed property will be sold at public sale after published notice, that the recipient has the right to bid at that sale, and that after the sale and deduction of storage, advertising, and sale costs, the remaining money is paid to the county and may be claimed within one year; or, alternatively, a statement that because the property is believed to be worth less than $700, it may be kept, sold, or destroyed without further notice if not reclaimed in time. Civil Code § 1985 sets out a separate statutory notice form for use when the person being notified is not the former tenant but someone else the landlord reasonably believes to be an owner of the property; a notice given in substantially that form likewise satisfies § 1983.

The landlord must exercise reasonable care in storing the property, but is not liable to the tenant or any other owner for any loss that was not caused by the landlord's own deliberate or negligent act.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 1987(a) requires the landlord to release the described property to the former tenant or, at the landlord's option, to another person reasonably believed to be its owner, if that person pays the reasonable cost of storage and takes possession by the date specified in the notice. Under § 1987(b), if the property was not released and the notice stated it would be sold at public sale, the landlord must still release it to the former tenant if the tenant claims it before the sale and pays the reasonable costs of storage, advertising, and sale incurred up to that point. Under § 1987(c), notwithstanding subdivision (a), the landlord must release the property to the former tenant without charging for storage if the property remained in the dwelling and the former tenant or reasonably-believed owner reclaims it within two days of vacating. Civil Code § 1990 governs how storage costs are assessed: a former tenant reclaiming property may be required to pay the reasonable costs of storage for all property remaining at the end of the tenancy that are unpaid at the time of the claim, while an owner other than the former tenant may be required to pay only for storage of the property in which that owner claims an interest; the landlord may not charge more than one person for the same costs; and if the landlord stores the property on the premises, the cost of storage is the fair rental value of the space reasonably required for that storage, with no cost assessed at all if the former tenant reclaims property stored on the premises within two days of vacating.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 1988(a) provides that personal property not released under § 1987 must be sold at public sale by competitive bidding — unless the landlord reasonably believes the total resale value of the unreleased property is less than $700, in which case the landlord may instead retain the property for personal use or dispose of it in any manner. The statute expressly permits the landlord or the tenant to bid on the property at the public sale. Under § 1988(b), notice of the time and place of a public sale must be published under Government Code § 6066 in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the sale will be held, with the last publication no less than five days before the sale, and that sale notice cannot be published before the deadline date specified in the § 1983 notice; the sale notice must describe the property adequately for its owner to identify it, subject to the same locked-container exception as the § 1983 notice. Under § 1988(c), after deducting the costs of storage, advertising, and sale, any unclaimed balance of the sale proceeds must be paid into the treasury of the county where the sale took place no later than 30 days after the sale; the former tenant or other owner may claim that balance within one year of the county's receipt of it by applying to the county treasurer or other designated county official, and if the county pays the balance to a claimant, neither the county nor its officers or employees are liable to any other claimant for the amount paid.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 1989 limits a landlord's liability for property handled under this chapter. Under § 1989(a), a landlord who releases property to the former tenant is not liable with respect to that property to any person. Under § 1989(b), a landlord who releases property under § 1987 to a reasonably-believed owner other than the former tenant is not liable to anyone who was given notice under § 1983, nor to anyone who was not given notice unless that person proves the landlord believed or reasonably should have believed they had an interest in the property and also knew or reasonably should have known their address. Section 1989(c) applies the identical two-part rule to property disposed of under § 1988. Separately, Civil Code § 1991 addresses how the notice required by this chapter interacts with a notice of belief of abandonment given under the different statute at Civil Code § 1951.3: where a landlord gives a tenant a notice of belief of abandonment under § 1951.3, the notice required by § 1983 of this chapter may — but need not — be given at the same time, even though the tenancy does not terminate until the period specified in the abandonment notice ends; and if both notices are given, they may, but need not, be combined into a single notice containing all the information each underlying statute requires.
